cells.note: Decided: a `move` inside a loop of a binding declared outside joins maybe-consumed at the back edge and may not flow into the next iteration's use (rejected); a body-local owned binding is auto-dropped at each iteration's end, on `continue`, and on every labeled jump that exits the body (§21.5); an owning iteration variable is discharged or auto-dropped on every body-exit edge, 'fall-through to the next iteration' included; the keep-the-best accumulator (`best := move cur;`) is §28.3's worked example. Hunted and closed: a `break` after a move (maybe-consumed after the loop, per-path drop), a §28.14 capture freeze across iterations (bound 2(a) records the loop residual). Open: the loop-carried shape that moves conditionally and reassigns at the body's end, `if c then Take(move r); end; r := new Res();`, is RC-E (R1×C7): whether the store is admitted at a maybe-consumed binding, and whether its drop is per path, is unstated. The shape is the natural spelling of a loop-carried owned binding, so the back edge carries the question into every iteration.

cells.rule: A5: "`using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable, never movable out" | §28.10: "`using var y := move x;` transfers a named owned local or `owned` parameter into a scope-bound binding: `y` takes over the disposal obligation and `x` is left moved-from" | §30.5: "not a `using var` binding: a `using var` cannot be moved out of ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), so a read of it is a borrow" | §31.1: "a *borrowed* class reference is not a valid operand" | §30.5: "the chained-slot arrangement **defers its disposal** from the frame's scope end to the outer task's teardown"
cells.cite: A5, A12, K3.4, §28.3 (Move semantics: `Wrap` example), §28.10 (Adopting a named owned binding; anonymous binding; compiler-introduced slot), §29.2, §30.5, §31.1; #5663
cells.note: Into R2: `using var y := move x;` (and `using var _ := move x;`, `out using var`, an owned arm-meet) adopts; the binding is then disposed at its block's end on every exit edge. Out of R2: every transfer is rejected (A5; the `Wrap` example's `move copy` error); the Pattern B await and `throw` of a `using var` read it as a borrow, so the operand is rejected or takes the borrowed-operand case. A12's Pattern A chaining is a disposal-timing deferral, not a move (L5's C10). The `for` desugaring's `__source`/`__enumerator` and the scoped await-bind slot are unnameable, so nothing can transfer out of them. #5663 is corpus catch-up of this decided text.

cells.rule: §28.10: "An expression whose arm-meet is **owned** — a `??`, an `if` expression, or an expression-position `case` over owned producers (the [K7](#sec-kernel-k7) meet; [§28.3](#sec-producers)) — is an owned producer for this section's admission" | §28.10: "and at least one arm is, the `using var` is **rejected** on that paragraph's ground" | §28.10: "the `using var` is a borrow-pin of the union of sources" | K7.5: "`null`-literal and bottom-typed (`throw`) arms absorb to the other arm's state."
cells.cite: K7, A7, §28.3 (Producers), §28.10 (owned arm-meet; all-owned-binding arm-meet rejection; borrow-pin), §20, §19.2; #5644, #5582, #5643
cells.note: A `using var` binding is never itself a join operand (it is non-reassignable and declared once), so C7 reaches it through its initializer: an owned meet adopts one obligation; an arm set made only of unmarked reads of named owned bindings is rejected (the compiler does not choose adopt-or-view); any other borrow arm makes it a borrow-pin over the union of sources, with no obligation. Hunted: `using var y := p ?? q;` over two borrow arms (#5643's hypothesis) is a borrow-pin by this text and disposes nothing, so #5643 is implementation; #5644/#5582 are catch-up of the rejection. An early `break` out of a branch that declared a `using var` runs its disposal on the jump (§21.5).

cells.rule: §28.10: "Disposal happens on every exit path: normal completion, `break`, `return`, or exception." | §30.5: "A bind inside a loop body pins to the loop *body*: per-iteration disposal, no accumulation across iterations." | §29.2: "Both `__source` and `__enumerator` are disposed on every exit path" | §21.5: "`using var`/`await using var` disposals and pending `finally` blocks run in reverse order of establishment"
cells.note: A `using var` declared in a loop body is a fresh binding per iteration (its block ends each iteration, and `continue`, `break` and labeled jumps are exit edges); one declared outside the loop is unaffected by the back edge, being non-reassignable (A5) and immovable. The scoped await-bind's hidden slot pins per iteration; the `for` desugaring's `__source`/`__enumerator` are established once per loop, outside the generated `while`, and disposed on every exit of the wrapper block. No accumulation or carried obligation is possible.

cells.rule: §28.3: "A temporary that had already transferred — into an `owned` parameter, a binding, an owned slot, or a return — is not disposed by this pass (its new owner's rules govern)" | K1.5: "Calls lend by default: an instance method's plain (non-`owned`) class-typed return is a borrow whose source is the receiver" | K8.4: "a borrow or frame that would escape it is **rejected, never lifetime-extended**" | §28.3: "the `Folded(src)` temporary is borrowed by `Sorted`, then disposed once the statement completes" | §28.6: "When a chain originates from a `new` expression — `new StringBuilder().Append("a").Append("b")` — the owned value produced by `new` is the root of the chain. The compiler treats the overall chain expression as owned (its root is a `new`)." | §28.6: "the chain as a whole must reach an owned location or `using var`, just as any other `new` expression must"
cells.cite: K1.5, K2.4, K3.13, K8.1, K8.4, §28.3 (Unbound owned temporaries; Producers; announcement table row 4), §28.6 (*Methods returning `this`*), §28.8.1 (raise from the consuming call), §35.5 (owning match over a temporary)
cells.note: Decided for every ordinary shape: a fresh producer transfers into an `owned` parameter, binding, owned slot, return or owning-match scrutinee without a marker and is then skipped by the boundary pass; a later argument's throw before entry disposes the already-produced temporary in the caller's unwind (the `Combine` example); the abandoned-store RHS is the unwind's temporary (§28.7). Conflict: §28.6's *Methods returning `this`* classifies a call chain rooted at `new` as **owned** and requires the chain to reach an owned location. K1.5 and announcement row 4 classify every intermediate plain instance return as a borrow of the receiver, the temporary, which is disposed at its K8 boundary (the `Folded(src).Sorted()` example), and K8.4 rejects binding or transferring it. The call site cannot know that a method returns `this`: the classification is type-announced, and A15/§29.1 decline exactly that per-body fact. Under §28.6's reading, `Keep(new Pool().First())`, with `First()` returning a field borrow, transfers the Pool's inner object to `Keep`. Then either the Pool temporary is disposed at the boundary and its cascade disposes the inner object a second time, or it is treated as transferred and leaks.

cells.rule: K7.1: "owned ⊓ owned = **owned**, obligation carried forward (for expression arms: exactly one arm's value exists at runtime, so exactly one obligation)" | K7.5: "`null`-literal and bottom-typed (`throw`) arms absorb to the other arm's state." | K8.5: "a binding whose initializer is an owned production is a **named unbound owned temporary** whose boundary is the atom — disposed at the atom's completion if undischarged" | K8.3: "the temporary survives arm selection, guard evaluation, and the selected arm's completion"
cells.cite: K7, K8.1–K8.5, §17.15, §20, §19.2, §28.3 (Producers `??`/if/atom rows; Unbound owned temporaries; `case` scrutinees extend the boundary), §35.5; #2123 (impl)
cells.note: An owned arm-meet of fresh producers is one owned temporary: only the selected arm is evaluated, so one obligation is produced and discharged at the full expression's end, or transferred if the meet sits in a transfer position. A `null` or `throw` arm absorbs. A mixed meet is rejected. A `case` scrutinee temporary lives through the selected arm. A binding-atom named temporary consumed on only some paths joins per K7.4 and is disposed per path at the atom boundary (#2123 is the implementation's conservative rejection of that decided shape). Editorial observation, not opened: §20 calls each branch 'a **full expression**' in its parse-precedence sense. K8 defines the lifetime boundary as maximal, so a branch is not one, but the K8 note's disclaimer names only §19.1's use of the phrase.

cells.rule: K8.2: "Conditions and guards are per-evaluation boundaries: temporaries never accumulate across iterations." | §28.3: "[K8.2](#sec-kernel-k8) makes each **evaluation** of a condition or pattern guard its own boundary, so condition temporaries never accumulate across iterations" | §29.2: "the wrapping `using var` assumes the disposal obligation and ensures the iterable is disposed when the loop ends"
cells.cite: K8.1, K8.2, K8.4, §21.3, §29.2, §28.3 (The full expression boundary)
cells.note: Each evaluation of a `while` condition or guard is its own boundary, and each body statement is its own full expression, so a temporary never crosses a back edge. A `for` source that is a fresh producer is bound once by the desugaring's `__source` and disposed at loop exit. A borrow of a temporary cannot be carried around a loop (K8.4 rejects its escape).

cells.rule: K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | §28.8.1: "A restoration placed in a `finally` satisfies the rule as well, when every throwable expression between the move and the store lies in that `try`'s protected block" | §28.8.1: "The store itself is into a moved-from location, so it is non-throwable" | §28.7: "A moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal" | §9.4: "a read of the vacated field through an alias of its holder, which the moved-from state of [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) does not track, reads the same state" | K9: "A field's obligation belongs to the object: it is discharged by the destructor cascade (owned fields, reverse declaration order) or by drop-on-overwrite, never by any scope's end"
cells.cite: K3.1, K9.1–K9.5, §23.3 (`set(owned)`), §28.5, §28.6, §28.7, §28.8.1 (restoration; exception paths; `finally` restoration; non-throwable inventory), §9.4 (move-only receivers: vacated storage), §22.9; #5725, #5667
cells.note: Decided: a store into an `owned` field or through `set(owned)` consumes marker-free (the new holder is the object, discharged by cascade or overwrite); `move x.f` is the one owned read, and K9.2 requires restoration on every path to the exit, exception edges included, at any receiver (#5725 is catch-up), with build-before-take keeping calls outside the window. Missing: the `finally`-restoration form admits arbitrary calls inside the window. A callee reaching the holder through `this` or another alias reads and writes the vacated class-typed field. The moved-from state is body-local, and §9.4 gives vacated storage a state only for a whole-value move of a **move-only** field. A callee's store into the vacated field is then overwritten by the restoration, which §28.7/§28.8.1 make a no-drop, 'non-throwable' store into a moved-from location, so that value leaks. If the move leaves the reference in place, the callee's drop-on-overwrite also disposes the object the taker owns. No flag, recorded clause or rule covers either use. #5667's own probe (`Helper()` inside the window) is this shape.

cells.rule: K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | §28.8.1: "The analysis reuses the control-flow graph and dominance frontiers that the existing definite-assignment analysis builds for non-defaultable locals" | K9: "no scope-end machinery ever touches it"
cells.cite: K9, K9.2, §28.8.1 (`Wrong`/`Right`/`Right2`; Loops and conditional control flow), §28.10 (field-arm meets), §28.6
cells.note: A field is object state, so no join merges its obligation. What C7 reaches is the restoration obligation after a `move x.f`, which is per path ('the false branch of `if replace`' is the stated error), and an arm that reads a field, which is a borrow arm (an owned field adopts only as `move o.f` under restoration, §28.10). A `move` inside one arm of an if-expression (`(if c then move _f else new R())`) is a fresh-producer arm, and restoration is owed on the selected path. No escape found.

cells.rule: §28.8.1: "Loops that may execute zero times do not satisfy the rule" | K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | K9.5: "drop-on-overwrite (K3.11) is RHS-first, so a throwing RHS leaves the slot untouched and still-owned"
cells.note: A field moved before a loop and restored only inside it is rejected (the loop may run zero times); a move and restoration in the same iteration is admitted with the window non-throwable. Reassigning an owned field inside a loop drops the displaced value each iteration (RHS-first). Nothing is carried around the back edge, because K9.2 is per path. The `finally`-window escape (RC-A) is not loop-specific.

cells.rule: §28.11: "after `move coll[i]` with a non-constant `i`, the *entire collection* is treated as having one or more slots in moved-from state" | §28.11: "`coll[j] := value` for any `j` (treated as restoration of one slot if `j` matches the moved index, or as unrelated reassignment otherwise)" | K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | §15.3: "auto-dispose on a moved-from slot is not defined" | §28.11: "a constant, or a local read not reassigned between — the per-slot precision the moved-from tracking below uses" | §28.11: "The compiler's per-slot moved-from tracking is what makes this distinguishable from a non-moved-from slot, where the setter does dispose the previous value."
cells.cite: K3.1, K9.1–K9.2, §28.11 (slot policy; owning collections; `move` on a collection slot; indexer setter on a moved-from slot), §28.8.1, stdlib §4.5, §4.14, §4.21; #5735
cells.note: Decided: ingress members take `owned`; an indexer-set drops the displaced element (and not at a slot moved-from by this body); `Pop*`/`Drain` hand ownership out in one step; `move coll[i]` at a constant or a not-reassigned local index is tracked per slot under K9.2. Conflict: after `move coll[e]` at a non-constant index, the whole collection is 'maybe moved', and §28.11 lists `coll[j] := value` 'for any `j`' as an admissible restoration. K9.2 requires the moved slot itself to be reassigned, and §15.3 leaves auto-dispose on a moved-from slot undefined. A store at an unrelated index therefore satisfies the conservative check at exit while the moved slot is still a hole. The cascade then meets it: depending on the unstated runtime representation, it disposes the taker's object a second time or reads null through a non-null `T` indexer. In the same shape, a store at the moved index's *spelling* after the local was reassigned is treated as a moved-from overwrite and skips the drop of the live element there. RC-A also reaches this row: a slot moved under a `finally` restoration is writable through the collection by a callee, and the restoring store does not drop.

cells.rule: K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | §28.11: "The field-restoration rule applies ([K9.2](#sec-kernel-k9), with per-slot tracking): the slot must be reassigned before the surrounding method exits." | §28.11: "the dominating-kill shape of [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s use-after-dispose warning, with the kill on the collection rather than on the binding"
cells.note: Slots are not scope state. A `move coll[i]` in one branch owes restoration on that branch's paths to the exit, and an element borrow joined across a conditional `Clear()`/`RemoveAt` is outside the dominating-kill warning and falls to K4.1's flag (the indexer row: 'checked-mode backstop'). An if-expression arm `move coll[i]` is a fresh-producer arm with restoration owed on its selected path. No escape beyond RC-B's non-constant index.

cells.rule: §28.11: "after `move coll[i]` with a non-constant `i`, the *entire collection* is treated as having one or more slots in moved-from state" | §28.11: "`coll[j] := value` for any `j` (treated as restoration of one slot if `j` matches the moved index, or as unrelated reassignment otherwise)" | §28.11: "a constant, or a local read not reassigned between — the per-slot precision the moved-from tracking below uses" | K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | §29.2: "the typical pattern for "consume every slot" uses `[N owned]T?` and assigns `null` after each move"
cells.cite: K9.2, §28.11 (`move` on a collection slot), §29.2 (note 4), §29.12, stdlib §4.5 (`PopAt`, `GrowTo`, `Clear` implementation sketches)
cells.note: Decided: per-iteration `move pool[i]` with an immediate restoration at the same not-reassigned index (the stdlib's own `PopAt`/`GrowTo`/`Clear` loops) is per-slot and sound, and `Drain()` iteration hands each element to an owned iteration variable. Conflict (RC-B): the loop is where the index changes. With `while k < n do var t := move pool[k]; k := k + 1; pool[k - 1] := …; end;` the restoring index is a computed expression, so the analysis is conservative, and a store 'for any `j`' counts as restoration, so the per-path K9.2 guarantee is not delivered. The loop-variable form (`for var i …`, freshly bound per iteration) is the decided spelling.

cells.rule: K3.12: "for move-only values ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), any store into an owning location" | §15.3: "A **whole-value** move — a plain binding, a plain argument, a return — creates no such obligation on a **local**" | §35.5: "the consumed binding is left **moved-from** when the construct completes" | §28.8.1: "A restoration placed in a `finally` satisfies the rule as well, when every throwable expression between the move and the store lies in that `try`'s protected block" | §28.7: "A moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal" | §9.4: "a read of the vacated field through an alias of its holder, which the moved-from state of [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) does not track, reads the same state"
cells.note: Decided: unmarked assignment, plain passing and return move a move-only value (marker rejected); `case move c` consumes and routes payloads at selection, with the remainder disposed at construct completion or in the unwind (trace d); a whole-value move of a local leaves no hole, and one of a field takes K9.2 plus §9.4's disposed state (#5652/#5642/#5541 are catch-up of that text); move-only `ref`/`out` locations are barred (#5565 family). Hunted: an exception out of an owning-match arm after partial routing (trace d: the routed binding is unwound, the rest disposed with the consumed value). Missing (RC-A): a **slot** move of an owning-inline-array field restored in a `finally` leaves a slot no state covers, which a callee can read or overwrite through the holder. The restoration store, into a moved-from location, does not drop, so a callee's slot store leaks. The same holds for a callee's *whole-value* store into a field §9.4 left in the disposed state, overwritten by the restoration. RC-C applies too: `Sink(arr[0], arr)` borrows a slot of `arr` in the same call that moves `arr` unmarked.

cells.rule: §28.3: "An **unmarked** read of a named owned binding remains a **borrow** arm (K3.13 — no silent consume)" | §28.3: "Local-variable read `x` where `x` is owned (a class-typed owned local, or a local of move-only value type per [§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types))" | §20: "When the branches are class-typed, the expression's ownership is the arm-meet of [§28.3](#sec-producers)'s producers table" | §15.3: "The one position at which a move-only operand *is* marked is the owning-match scrutinee `case move c of …`" | §15.3: "A move-only value binding has no borrow reading to disambiguate — copies are forbidden, so the plain binding can only move" | K3.4: "the **marked arm transfer**: `move x` as an if-expression branch or an expression-`case` arm result"
cells.note: Decided: statement-level joins of a move-only local follow K7 (a conditional whole-value move or `case move` joins maybe-consumed, auto-drop per path); an owning-match arm binding is per-arm. Ambiguous: an if-expression branch or expression-`case` arm (and a `??` operand over an owning `C?`) that names a move-only binding. The producers row makes the unmarked read 'a borrow arm', and the local-read row includes move-only locals. §15.3 says a plain move-only binding 'can only move' and that the owning-match scrutinee is 'the one position' where a move-only operand is marked, which bars K3.4's marked arm; §20 scopes its ownership rule to class-typed branches. Reading 1: `var y := (if c then a else b);` binds a borrow (a and b stay owned and auto-drop), and no conditional selection of two move-only values is writable except by statement. Reading 2: the arm moves the selected binding (per-path moved-from, as K3.12 moves at every owning store). An implementation that classifies the arms as borrows but binds `y` by move (K3.12) disposes the selected value twice. Reassignment after a conditional move is RC-E.

cells.rule: K7.4: "owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = **maybe-consumed** — unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path" | §28.11: "`arr[j] := value` for any `j` (for nullable forms, `arr[j] := null` is also a valid restoration that marks slots empty)" | §28.11: "after `move coll[i]` with a non-constant `i`, the *entire collection* is treated as having one or more slots in moved-from state" | §29.2: "Iterating an `[N owned]T` non-nullable owning array and moving from every slot without restoration is therefore rejected"
cells.cite: K7.4, K9.2, §15.1.1, §15.3, §28.11 (inline-array restoration bullet), §29.2 (direct-indexed sources, note 4)
cells.note: Decided: a move-only local whole-value-moved inside a loop body and declared outside it is maybe-consumed at the back edge (rejected); a move-only iteration-scoped local is auto-disposed per iteration; a direct-indexed loop over an owning inline array may `move arr[i]` at the loop variable and must restore before the exit. Conflict (RC-B): §28.11's inline-array bullet admits `arr[j] := value` 'for any `j`' as restoration after a non-constant-index move, against K9.2's per-slot requirement. The array's own exit pass then meets an unrestored slot ('auto-dispose on a moved-from slot is not defined').

cells.rule: K3.8: "the operand of `throw` ([§31.1](#sec-the-throw-operand)) | none — the keyword announces | **moved-from** | **unfrozen** (K4.2, K5.3)† | after the matching catch arm completes, or at termination if uncaught" | §31.1: "the runtime's dispose-after-arm sets the disposed flag, so a borrow surviving the handler faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode" | §31.1: "Inside a catch arm, the bound exception variable (`var ex: Exception` in the arm pattern) is a **borrow** of the in-flight exception" | K3.2: "the task's result, [§30.5](#sec-result-lifetime-and-task-disposal)'s Pattern B transfer and Pattern A kind 1 (disposed by the awaiter or by the task's teardown, as §30.5 states)"
cells.note: Into the runtime: `throw x` and `throw new E()` transfer to the exception machinery (disposed after the matching arm, or at termination), a surviving borrow being K4.1-backstopped (the quoted sentence); a returned result transfers into the task's slot (K3.2; #5704/#5703 are catch-up). Out of the runtime: a Pattern B await moves the result to the awaiter. A `catch` binding is a borrow (not assignable to an owned field, not returnable owned, not an owned argument), and the bare re-raise hands the instance back. The two owner-owned exemptions (cached `TypeInitializationException`, a faulted task's fault) are never transferred. Await-side details are L5's C10.

cells.rule: §28.3: "A *conditional* kill of any row joins to **maybe-consumed** ([K7.4](#sec-kernel-k7)) — one clause, applying to every row." | K7.4: "owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = **maybe-consumed** — unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path" | K3.5: "at the await, on all outgoing edges including fault and cancel"
cells.note: An owned task local awaited (Pattern B) or thrown on one branch joins maybe-consumed and is dropped per path at scope end. An exception's ownership never meets a join, being the runtime's from the throw to the arm's completion, and a catch binding is a borrow whose lifetime is the arm. A `throw` arm in an if-expression absorbs (K7.5). Exactly-once holds on both joined paths.

cells.rule: K7.4: "owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = **maybe-consumed** — unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path" | §28.3: "join to **maybe-consumed** the variable may not be read, borrowed from, or consumed, and may not flow around a loop back edge into any use, while scope-end auto-drop applies per-path" | §30.5: "A bind inside a loop body pins to the loop *body*: per-iteration disposal, no accumulation across iterations."
cells.note: A task declared outside a loop and Pattern-B-awaited inside it is maybe-consumed at the back edge (rejected). Per-iteration tasks (scoped await-bind, body locals) are disposed per iteration. A `throw` inside a loop body transfers its operand once; the jump discipline unwinds body-local holders.

cells.rule: §29.8: "An iterator method may take `owned` parameters. The state machine takes ownership at construction time." | §29.3: "An iterator method's return type is `IEnumerable<T>` (re-iterable: each call to `GetEnumerator()` runs the body again from the start)" | K6.3: "callee-side, the unmarked mint-announcing return type transfers the container like an `owned` return" | K3.7: "the operand of `yield return` in an owning iterator ([§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership)) | none — the declared owning interface announces | **moved-from**" | §29.8: "Moving the parameter out of the iterator (via an `owned` argument call or a `using var` re-bind) puts the parameter in the moved-from state"
cells.note: Decided: a frame is minted owned at every call and transferred by an unmarked mint-announcing return; an owning iterator's `yield return x` consumes `x` (frozen); a frame-resident owned local or parameter moved out by the body is skipped by the frame's teardown; a single-use enumerator or a task holds its `owned` arguments to completion or settlement. Missing: an `owned` argument passed to a **re-iterable** iterator. 'The state machine takes ownership' does not say whether the new holder is the enumerable or each enumerator, though each `GetEnumerator()` re-runs the body. This is the pilot's R8×C11 root cause seen from the transfer side; not re-filed.

cells.rule: §29.7: "**in reverse order of establishment, exactly as if the body had exited at the suspension point**" | K7.4: "owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = **maybe-consumed** — unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path"
cells.note: An iterator or async body is an ordinary body for K7, and its frame-resident locals join exactly as R1's do. On early disposal at a suspension point, §29.7 runs the pending cleanups as if the body exited there, so a maybe-consumed frame-resident local is dropped per path. Joins never merge the frame's own obligation, a value held by the caller.

cells.rule: K7.4: "owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = **maybe-consumed** — unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path" | §29.7: "Runs the pending cleanup actions active at the point of suspension" | §29.2: "the iteration variable is either discharged by the program or auto-dropped with the warning"
cells.note: A loop around `yield return` inside an iterator body uses the same back-edge rule as R1. A loop-carried frame-resident owned binding moved conditionally is rejected at the back edge, or meets RC-E if reassigned. Abandonment mid-loop runs the per-iteration holders' cleanups. A consumer loop's owning iteration variable is discharged per iteration. No frame-specific escape found in C8.

cells.rule: K9.4: "static owned fields admit no `move`: the restoration obligation is scoped to a single method, and static state is observable across method boundaries, so no per-method window can cover it" | §22.12: "slot stores, `move arr[j]`, and per-slot restoration follow [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays) unchanged" | §22.12: "assigning a fresh owned value into an admitted mutable static discharges the producer" | §28.8.1: "A restoration placed in a `finally` satisfies the rule as well, when every throwable expression between the move and the store lies in that `try`'s protected block" | §28.7: "A moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal"
cells.cite: K9.4, §22.12 (rule 2 form (iv), Ownership/Overwrite bullets, rule 4, notes (g)–(h)), §22.13, §28.8.1, §28.3 (*Static stores*)
cells.note: Decided: a `static owned readonly` field takes its value once from a fresh producer (disposed in the exit pass); `move T.f` of a static field is rejected (K9.4); a fresh value stored into an admitted non-`owned` static discharges the producer (exempt: process-lived). Missing (RC-A, statics form): form (iv) admits `move arr[j]` on a static owning inline array with per-slot restoration, which K9.4's own ground rejects for whole fields ('static state is observable across method boundaries'). Under a `finally` restoration, any method of any class can read or overwrite the vacated slot while it is moved-from, and the restoring store does not drop, so such a store leaks. The cross-domain reach is form (iv)'s recorded rule-4 confinement obligation. The same-domain window has no clause.

cells.rule: K9: "no scope-end machinery ever touches it" | K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | §22.12: "overwriting an admitted mutable static never disposes the displaced referent"
cells.note: Statics are never scope state: no join merges a static's obligation, and a branch-dependent overwrite of an admitted mutable static never drops (exempt, process-lived to exit). The one per-path question, restoration of a form-(iv) slot moved in one branch, is K9.2's per-path rule. Not n/a: the slot-move path is real; it is decided.

cells.rule: §28.11: "`arr[j] := value` for any `j` (for nullable forms, `arr[j] := null` is also a valid restoration that marks slots empty)" | §28.11: "after `move coll[i]` with a non-constant `i`, the *entire collection* is treated as having one or more slots in moved-from state" | §22.12: "slot stores, `move arr[j]`, and per-slot restoration follow [§15.1.1](#sec-owning-inline-arrays) unchanged" | §22.12: "a whole-field reassignment reachable with provably non-moved-from slots warns, naming the slots at risk"
cells.note: Decided: whole-field reassignment of a form-(iv) static inside a loop keeps the displaced slots alive to exit (exempt, warned), and statics carry nothing across a back edge. Conflict, inherited through form (iv)'s 'follow §15.1.1 unchanged': a loop that moves `Registry.Slots[k]` at a computed index meets RC-B's 'for any `j`' restoration (see R6×C8). It is worse here because the hole is visible to every method of the program until the restoration runs.

cells.rule: §28.1: "Such values carry no disposal obligation to transfer" | §28.9: "Capturing an *owned* class-typed local does **not** transfer ownership into the closure" | K1.6: "Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation"
cells.note: `owned` over a runtime-managed type is a compile error (or erased at a generic substitution), the transfer marker on a non-owned operand is rejected, and copying a function value, string or box moves nothing. Hunted: smuggling an owned referent into a closure (the capture is a borrow, bounded by the local's scope; the closure may not consume it, §28.3 *Captured owned bindings*); boxing an owning choice or owning inline array (rejected, §35.8/§8.6). No leak through the exemption.

cells.rule: §28.9: "the closure may not assign to, transfer from, or dispose the captured binding, and may not outlive that scope" | K5.5: "and this is why a closure may not consume its captured owned bindings (K2 + decidability)"
cells.cite: K1.6, K5.5, K7.2, §28.3 (*Captured owned bindings*; closure bullet), §28.9
cells.note: A meet of function values, strings or boxes moves no obligation. Hunted: a closure over an owned local that survives a conditional move of that local (`var f := lambda() => x.N; if c then Take(move x); end; f();`) is rejected by the freeze, the closure being a live local borrow of `x`.

cells.rule: §28.9: "a closure cannot extend the lifetime of an owned class instance, so reclaiming the closure never leaves a destructor un-run" | §21.4: "The loop variable is freshly bound on each iteration: a lambda captured inside the body sees the value of that specific iteration."
cells.note: A closure created per iteration over a per-iteration owned local cannot be carried around the back edge into a wider-scoped holder (borrow escape, K2.3). §28.14's loop residual (bound 2(a)/(b)) is recorded as a non-hole. No runtime-managed value keeps an owned referent alive across iterations.

cells.rule: K4.2: "**Site-announced kills.** A kill that is both **keyword-visible at the kill site** and **flag-backstopped** is **site-announced**, and is permitted while borrows of the value live: the announcement is the reader's notice and the flag is the safety net." | K1: "Scope-end machinery skips it, and a straight-line read falls under [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s use-after-dispose warning regime rather than the moved-from error." | §28.2: "The compiler additionally **must** emit a compile-time warning when a local variable is used (read, borrowed from, or consumed) after an explicit `Dispose()` or direct `DisposeAsync()` call" | §28.2: "A *conditional* kill is treated more strictly: at a join of an explicitly-disposed path with a still-owned path the variable is **maybe-consumed** and a later use is a compile error" | §28.7: "then, if the previous value is live (non-null and not moved-from — the per-slot tracking [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)'s indexer-set rule already defines), it is disposed" | §28.3: "Two states qualify, and no others: an **uninitialized** local" | §28.2: "A further `Dispose()` call remains a no-op, not an error, in both modes." | §28.4: "After step 3 has propagated to the root of the hierarchy, the object's memory is reclaimed — immediately, or deferred under checked disposal mode's quarantine latitude"
cells.note: The kill itself is decided: an owned local or `owned` parameter is discharged at the K3.9 call or discard, left explicitly-disposed, skipped by scope-end and unwind machinery; a dominated later use (a `move x` or owned argument included) draws §28.2's warning and every member access through any alias faults under K4.1, while a conditional kill joins to maybe-consumed (error). Open: reassigning the explicitly-disposed binding (`c.Dispose(); c := new Res();`) is neither adoption (§28.3 names only uninitialized and polymorphic-null) nor stated as state-matched, and under §28.7's literal liveness test the displaced, already-disposed value is disposed again, warning-free; §28.2 promises that second call is a no-op 'in both modes' while §28.4/§28.12 reclaim the block immediately in an unchecked build, so the language itself issues a Dispose() on released memory (L4-RC1).

cells.rule: §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type." | K1: "Scope-end machinery skips it, and a straight-line read falls under [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s use-after-dispose warning regime rather than the moved-from error." | §28.10: "an explicit `Dispose()` of the source is permitted, and a read through the pinned binding afterwards raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode" | A5: "`using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable, never movable out" | K4.2: "**Site-announced kills.** A kill that is both **keyword-visible at the kill site** and **flag-backstopped** is **site-announced**, and is permitted while borrows of the value live: the announcement is the reader's notice and the flag is the safety net." | §28.6: "`Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error."
cells.note: A `using var` is an owned receiver (§28.6): an explicit `Dispose()`/discard leaves it explicitly-disposed and its scope end skips it, and A5 forbids reassignment, so no second language-issued disposal arises. A borrow-pin owns nothing (`Dispose()` through it is the borrow error), and a site-announced kill of the pinned source is unfrozen with every later read through the pin flag-backstopped. The compiler-introduced slots (`__source`, `__enumerator`, the scoped await-bind slot) are unnameable, so no explicit kill reaches them; a kill of the source they borrow is the pin case. Hunted: kill-then-reassign (A5 rejects), move-after-kill (A5 rejects). #4954/#4882 are implementation escapes of the decided rules.

cells.rule: §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type." | §28.3: "the **Spelling**, **Post-state**, and **Frozen** columns describe the case where the consumed operand is an owned **binding** — a local or an `owned` parameter — since a fresh producer or unbound temporary in the same position involves no binding" | §28.3: "not bound to any name, not `move`d, and not returned, but used only by *borrowing* operations within the expression — as the receiver of a further call" | §28.3: "A temporary that is instead bound (to a `var`/`using var`), `move`d, returned, or transferred into an owning location is governed by the corresponding transfer or discharge rule and is **not** disposed under this rule (it would otherwise be disposed twice)." | §28.2: "A further `Dispose()` call remains a no-op, not an error, in both modes." | §28.4: "After step 3 has propagated to the root of the hierarchy, the object's memory is reclaimed — immediately, or deferred under checked disposal mode's quarantine latitude"
cells.note: The discard `_ := Make();` is decided (one disposal at the statement end, nothing can name the value afterwards). The call spelling `Make().Dispose()` is admitted on an unbound owned temporary (§28.6) but the text gives two readings of what follows: the consume table's Position column covers 'any owned value', making the call a K3.9 consume the K8 boundary skips; §28.3 defines the temporary as one used only by borrowing operations 'as the receiver of a further call' and lists bind/move/return/transfer, not explicit disposal, as the exits from the boundary pass, so the boundary disposes it again. Exactly-once of the destructor holds either way (§28.2 idempotence); under reading 2 the second call lands on a block an unchecked build has already released (L4-RC1).

cells.rule: §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type." | §28.6: "The call is an **early release point**, not a discharge of the slot's obligation: the slot keeps its reference and its [K9](#sec-kernel-k9) obligation, and the containing object's teardown still runs the cascade over it ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) step 2), where the second call is [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s no-op" | §28.6: "at a **trivial-dispose** slot type, the compiler's single free stays at the holder's release point, which [§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes) already fixes as the containing object's teardown, the explicit call having performed logical disposal only." | §28.6: "so the reader is [K4.1](#sec-kernel-k4)'s backstop: a member access through it raises `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode and is undefined unchecked" | §28.7: "An explicit `field.Dispose();` before the assignment remains legal and behavior-preserving — `Dispose` is idempotent ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)), so the implicit disposal of an already-disposed value is a no-op." | §28.2: "A further `Dispose()` call remains a no-op, not an error, in both modes." | §28.4: "After step 3 has propagated to the root of the hierarchy, the object's memory is reclaimed — immediately, or deferred under checked disposal mode's quarantine latitude" | §28.12: "physical reclamation runs **exactly once, immediately after whichever logical-disposal path completes**" | §28.2: "The two modes give identical observable behavior for every program that never uses a disposed instance."
cells.cite: K3.9, K4.1, K5.6, K9, K9.2, §28.2, §28.4, §28.6 (Who may call Dispose(); early release), §28.7, §28.12; changelog #4366
cells.note: The declaring type may dispose an owned field (any instance it reaches); the call is an early release, the slot keeps its reference and K9 obligation, the teardown cascade (or a later drop-on-overwrite) calls Dispose() again as §28.2's no-op, and later reads through the field are K4.1-backstopped (no static diagnostic). Conflict: §28.2 says that second call is a no-op 'in both modes', but §28.4 and §28.12 release the heap block 'immediately' after logical disposal in an unchecked build. The cascade's no-op is therefore a Dispose() on released memory in a program that never uses the disposed instance itself, against §28.2's identical-behavior claim. The trivial-dispose case alone is carved: the explicit call is logical only, and the free stays at the holder's release point (L4-RC1).

cells.rule: §28.6: "an element borrow of an **owning** collection (`pool[i].Dispose()` — use `Remove`/`RemoveAt`, the indexer-set, or `move coll[i]`, whose forms keep the slot state coherent" | §28.3 (producers): "the borrow is additionally valid only until the slot is mutated (an indexer-set, `Remove*`, or `Clear` disposes the referent" | §28.11: "The compiler **must warn** when a local holding such a borrow is used (read, borrowed from, or passed) after a call on the **same collection binding** that **disposes the borrowed element** and **dominates the use on every path**" | K4.1: "**The backstop.** Disposal is idempotent and flag-setting; in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) any later use through any alias faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException`, and unchecked mode is the same language with the check elided." | §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type."
cells.cite: K3.1, K4.1, K4.2, K5.6, §28.3 (indexer row), §28.6, §28.11 (slot policy; use-after-removal warning; move on a slot), stdlib §4.5–§4.12, §4.21; #4777 (impl)
cells.note: User code cannot dispose a slot in place: `pool[i].Dispose()` is a borrow-receiver error, and the owning-collection-slot admission in §28.6 reaches only the collection's own declaring-type code. The slot kills are `Remove`/`RemoveAt`/`Clear`/the indexer-set (each disposes once and closes or refills the slot, so the cascade never meets the value again) and `Dispose()` of the container. A surviving element borrow is warned on the dominating same-binding shape (§28.11) and is K4.1-backstopped otherwise; keyed `OwningDictionary.Remove(k)` is a recorded chosen silence under the same flag. An owned-field container's own early release is R4/C9's shape (L4-RC1).

cells.rule: §35.9: "`Dispose` stays off the surface everywhere: choices do not implement `IDisposable`" | §17.13: "For a **move-only value** (an owning inline array `[N owned]T?`/`[N owned]T`, or an owning-classified choice) its owned slots — for a choice, the active case's owned payloads — are disposed in the usual order." | §17.13: "`x` is thereafter treated exactly as explicitly disposed" | §9.4: "In checked disposal mode a read of the value in that state — through an in-place `this`, or through a borrowing-match binding of it, an owning inline array's slot reads, iteration and compiler-provided operations ([§15.1.2](#sec-members-and-operations)) included — faults as `DisposedAccessException`" | §15.3: "each slot of the displaced value that is **live** — non-null and not moved-from, §28.7's liveness test — is disposed, **in reverse slot order**" | §28.2: "A further `Dispose()` call remains a no-op, not an error, in both modes." | §28.4: "After step 3 has propagated to the root of the hierarchy, the object's memory is reclaimed — immediately, or deferred under checked disposal mode's quarantine latitude"
cells.note: Neither move-only kind has `Dispose()`; the explicit kill is the discard of a named binding, which disposes the slots / active payloads once and leaves the binding explicitly-disposed (scope end skips it); a vacated field or destroyed holder is in §9.4's disposed state, whose reads fault in checked mode, and slot objects carry their own K4.1 flags. Open on L4-RC1's ground: a whole-value reassignment after the discard (`_ := arr; arr := …;`) runs §15.3's per-slot pass over every non-null, non-moved-from displaced slot, so each already-disposed slot object is disposed a second time — a no-op by §28.2, a Dispose() on released memory in an unchecked build. The #5652/#5642/#5541 tracking rows implement the decided disposed state.

cells.rule: §31.1: "the runtime's dispose-after-arm sets the disposed flag, so a borrow surviving the handler faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode" | §31.1: "Inside a catch arm, the bound exception variable (`var ex: Exception` in the arm pattern) is a **borrow** of the in-flight exception" | K3.5: "at the await, on all outgoing edges including fault and cancel" | §30.5: "any await of an already-disposed task raises `InvalidOperationException`" | §30.9: "The exception is disposed **exactly once, by the task that owns it, when the task is disposed**" | §28.6: "`Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error."
cells.cite: K3.5, K3.8, K4.2, K5.3, §28.6, §30.5, §30.9 (Fault ownership), §31.1 (throw operand; Exception ownership), §31.2
cells.note: `throw x` and Pattern B `await t` are site-announced kills with stated moments (after the matching arm completes / at the await on every edge); the operand binding is moved-from, and surviving borrows are flag-backstopped (§31.1's dispose-after-arm sets the flag). A catch-arm binding is a borrow, so disposing it is the borrow-receiver error, and a field-stored borrow of it is the K4.3 field-held clause. A task-owned fault exception is disposed exactly once with its task, and an await after an explicit task disposal raises InvalidOperationException. Hunted: dispose-then-throw (warning, then a member access in the handler faults), dispose-then-await (InvalidOperationException), a borrow of the exception kept past the arm (flag).

cells.rule: §29.7: "a `MoveNext()` after disposal is an ordinary instance member access on a disposed instance and is governed by [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)" | §28.3 (Frame locals): "The site-announced kills of a carried borrow stay unfrozen under the flag: every read the frame makes through it is a member access" | §30.5: "any await of an already-disposed task raises `InvalidOperationException`" | §29.1: "a `Dispose()`/`DisposeAsync()` after an advance whose value was never taken **disposes the pending value**" | K6.4: "A **task's** are not traced by K5: their outlives-obligation is the K4.3-recorded settlement clause"
cells.note: An explicit Dispose() of an enumerator or lazy-query frame runs §29.7's pending cleanup once and transitions to completed; a later `MoveNext()` is a member access on a disposed instance (K4.1). An explicit Dispose() of an unsettled task attaches the result-disposing continuation, and a later await raises InvalidOperationException. The enumerator's untaken pending value is disposed with it (§29.1). A site-announced kill of a source the frame carries is unfrozen and every frame read through it is a flag-checked member access (K5.5; #5698 tracks the implementation). The re-iterable iterator's `owned` parameter is filed as a route cell under the pilot's R8/C11 root cause; #4827 (wrong slot on explicit Dispose) is an implementation defect of this decided cell.

cells.rule: §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type." | K2: "static storage — the one distinguished *always-live* source (process-lived, disposed only at exit, [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order));" | §28.3 (producers): "every admissible form keeps its referents alive to process exit" | K9.4: "static owned fields admit no `move`: the restoration obligation is scoped to a single method, and static state is observable across method boundaries" | §22.13: "Static `owned` fields are disposed at program exit, after `Main` completes" | §28.2: "A further `Dispose()` call remains a no-op, not an error, in both modes." | §28.4: "After step 3 has propagated to the root of the hierarchy, the object's memory is reclaimed — immediately, or deferred under checked disposal mode's quarantine latitude"
cells.cite: K2, K4.1, K9.4, §22.12 rule 4, §22.13 (Disposal of static owned fields), §28.3 (Static field access row; Static stores), §28.6 (Who may call Dispose()), §28.2, §28.4
cells.note: §28.6 admits an explicit Dispose() or direct DisposeAsync() of a `static owned` field by code of its declaring type. K2 and the producers' static rows classify every static read as always-live storage 'disposed only at exit', whose referents stay alive to process exit. On that ground, static-storage-sourced borrows are stored into any field or static with no residual and no trust-report entry. After an early disposal those borrows outlive their referent with no recorded clause: within one domain K4.1 still faults the use, across domains see R9/C13. The exit pass then disposes the field a second time, which is L4-RC1's unchecked-mode hazard. K9.4 bars `move` of the same field on the cross-method-observability ground, which applies equally to an early disposal (L4-RC2).

cells.rule: K1.6: "Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation" | §28.3: "a closure cannot consume, reassign, or dispose a captured owned binding" | §8.6: "Move-only value types — owning inline arrays (`[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?`) and owning-classified choices ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) — cannot be boxed."
cells.cite: K1.6, §8.6, §28.1, §28.2 (summary: runtime-managed `Dispose()` is a no-op), §28.3 (Captured owned bindings), §28.9
cells.note: Runtime-managed values carry no classification or obligation, so an explicit `Dispose()` on one is the no-op and no use-after question arises. Hunted for an exemption leaking into an obligation path: a closure cannot dispose (or consume) a captured owned binding; a closure over a borrow of an owned local that is later explicitly disposed reaches the object only through member accesses, which K4.1 flags; move-only values cannot be boxed, so no box hides an owned slot from the kill.

cells.rule: §30.14: "the origin domain loses access **statically at the binding level** — the consumed binding is left moved-from, and the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) rejects the transfer while any local borrow of that binding is live" | §30.14: "class-typed arguments are `owned` and are moved through the spawn into the entry's parameter." | K4.3: "**Recorded trust, or nothing.** Where an admission's temporal guarantee can neither be statically compared (K2.3) nor flag-backstopped — the domain clause ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s field-store bullet, clause 4): a borrowed-from object transferred to, or made reachable from, another domain stays alive, so no flag is ever set" | §28.3 cl.4: "A field-stored borrow of an object later moved across a domain boundary — directly, or through a different binding such as `move box.f` into a spawn argument or channel send — is *not* rejected by the consume-site freeze below" | §30.1: "every borrow source reaching an async call must outlive the settlement of the returned task"
cells.note: An owned binding crosses only as an `owned` spawn argument or channel `Send` (K3.3, frozen): the origin binding is moved-from, the receiving domain's `owned` parameter / Receive result discharges it, and a raise from the consuming call leaves it with the callee (§28.8.1). Indirect pre-transfer aliases (field-, collection-, comparer-held, pending-frame) are the K4.3-recorded domain clause, explicitly not flag-backstopped; the trust-admission report names them. Hunted: transfer after a dominating Dispose() (warned; the moved object's flag crosses with it under the spawn/channel happens-before edges), a live closure or frame over the binding (frozen), a pending task over it (§30.1 settlement clause).

cells.rule: A5: "`using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable, never movable out" | §30.14: "the origin domain loses access **statically at the binding level** — the consumed binding is left moved-from, and the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) rejects the transfer while any local borrow of that binding is live" | §30.14: "class-typed arguments are `owned` and are moved through the spawn into the entry's parameter."
cells.note: A `using var` (and every compiler-introduced slot of its kind) is never movable out, and a class value crosses a domain only as an owned transfer, so the holder itself cannot reach another domain; its borrow-pin form owns nothing and a borrow is never sendable. What a scoped binding sends (`sender.Send(BuildReport(1))`, a `Clone()` of a pinned handle) is a fresh value, R3/C13.

cells.rule: §30.14: "class-typed arguments are `owned` and are moved through the spawn into the entry's parameter." | §30.15: "A send that **faults** disposes its class-typed item before the exception surfaces" | §30.15: "Disposing the `Channel<T>` itself closes it immediately and disposes every undelivered class-typed item in reverse insertion order"
cells.note: A fresh temporary passed to an `owned` spawn argument or `Send` transfers at call entry and is discharged on the receiving side; a faulting send disposes the item before the exception surfaces, a channel disposes undelivered items in reverse insertion order, and a temporary whose consuming call is never entered is disposed by the caller's unwind. Plain spawn rows admit no class type, so no temporary crosses as a borrow.

cells.rule: §30.14 rule 2: "an owning-inline-array field (`[N owned]C` / `[N owned]C?`) whose element class is a sendable class type" | §28.3 cl.4: "A field-stored borrow of an object later moved across a domain boundary — directly, or through a different binding such as `move box.f` into a spawn argument or channel send — is *not* rejected by the consume-site freeze below" | K4.3: "**Recorded trust, or nothing.** Where an admission's temporal guarantee can neither be statically compared (K2.3) nor flag-backstopped — the domain clause ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s field-store bullet, clause 4): a borrowed-from object transferred to, or made reachable from, another domain stays alive, so no flag is ever set"
cells.note: An owned field crosses only inside its holder's owned transfer (transfer-closed rule 2 requires every owned field sendable), so its obligation moves with the tree and the receiving domain's teardown cascades over it; `move box.f` into a spawn argument or `Send` is an ordinary K9.2 take plus transfer. A borrow of the field's current value left in the origin domain is the recorded domain clause (not flag-backstopped), named by the trust-admission report.

cells.rule: §30.14: "an owning collection iff its element type is a sendable class type" | §30.14: "Moved-in items that were never processed are disposed by the runtime" | §30.15: "Disposing the `Channel<T>` itself closes it immediately and disposes every undelivered class-typed item in reverse insertion order"
cells.note: Sub-shapes: an owning collection crosses as one owned transfer iff its element type is sendable (its slots move with it, once); a borrowing collection of class elements is not sendable (rejected); `Parallel.*` over `owned items` moves the elements to workers and the runtime disposes unprocessed ones; a channel's buffered items are slots of the channel, disposed once on its disposal. A slot taken by `move coll[i]` into a spawn is the R4 domain-clause shape.

cells.rule: §30.14: "**Value types** are sendable iff they are not borrow-bearing ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)), not move-only ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), and **every component type is sendable**." | §30.14 rule 2: "an owning-inline-array field (`[N owned]C` / `[N owned]C?`) whose element class is a sendable class type" | §8.6: "Move-only value types — owning inline arrays (`[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?`) and owning-classified choices ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) — cannot be boxed."
cells.note: A move-only value is never sendable by itself (value-type rule) and cannot be boxed past the check, so a spawn argument, result or channel element of that type is rejected. As an owning-inline-array or owning-choice field of a sendable class it rides its holder's owned transfer and is disposed once by the receiving domain's cascade.

cells.rule: §30.14: "An exception that propagates out of the entry does not cross the boundary as an object" | §30.14: "The entry's task object never crosses the boundary: it lives and dies in the spawned domain" | §30.9: "The exception is disposed **exactly once, by the task that owns it, when the task is disposed**" | §30.15: "A send that **faults** disposes its class-typed item before the exception surfaces"
cells.note: No exception and no task object crosses: an entry's escaping exception is owned by the entry task in the spawned domain and disposed with it, while the join raises a fresh DomainFaultedException carrying copied strings; the join handle is an ordinary task of the spawning domain (Pattern B result transfer for `OwningTask<R>`). A pending `Receive` disposed before handoff gives the item back, and a faulting send disposes its item.

cells.rule: §30.14: "The entry's task object never crosses the boundary: it lives and dies in the spawned domain" | §30.1: "every borrow source reaching an async call must outlive the settlement of the returned task" | §28.3 cl.4: "A field-stored borrow of an object later moved across a domain boundary — directly, or through a different binding such as `move box.f` into a spawn argument or channel send — is *not* rejected by the consume-site freeze below" | K6.4: "A **task's** are not traced by K5: their outlives-obligation is the K4.3-recorded settlement clause"
cells.cite: K6, K6.4, K4.3, §28.3 (field-store cl.5), §30.1, §30.14 (Domain completion), stdlib §6.8
cells.note: Frames are interface- or Task-typed and never sendable, so no frame crosses; an `async` entry's task lives and dies in the spawned domain, and pending tasks left there continue under FireAndForget handling. A borrow a pending frame holds of an object later transferred to another domain is the §30.1 settlement clause's recorded domain extension (K4.3), not flag-backstopped.

cells.rule: §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type." | §22.12 rule 4: "the referenced instance is reachable from every domain, and confining its use to one domain — or ensuring its own internal synchronization — is the programmer's obligation (the checked-disposal backstop of [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract) applies; this is the singleton-with-resources pattern the warning text names)." | K4.3: "across domains the flag is no backstop, so the always-live holder admits only what lives as long as it does." | §28.3 (Static stores): "the source's owner can dispose it in one domain while another reads the static — a race the flag does not order and the domain clause cannot discharge, since no transfer or consume of the source ever happens." | §28.2: "they cannot arise across domains either, since domains share no mutable state" | §30.12: "in **checked disposal mode** the runtime must detect destruction of a lock with live guards (holders or waiters) and fault deterministically"
cells.note: A `static owned readonly` field is reachable from every domain. §28.6 lets its declaring type dispose it at any time, and the exit pass's single-thread guarantee covers only exit. Rule 4 names 'the checked-disposal backstop of §28.2' as the safety net. K4.3 and the Static-stores bullet state the opposite for exactly this race: across domains the flag is no backstop. §28.2 even assumes no cross-domain disposal can arise. For the warning-suppression set (`Mutex`, `Semaphore`, `SharedEventSource<T>`, `CancellationTokenSource`, `FrozenArray<T>`) the program is warning-free, and no K4.3 clause records it. Only `Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>` carry a named checked-mode detection (§30.12), and it covers live guards, not a later acquisition (L4-RC2).

cells.rule: §30.14: "**`string`** and **`Type`** are sendable; each crosses as a shared reference, which is safe because both are immutable" | §30.14: "**Function-typed values are never sendable**: their captures are borrows of the origin domain's scopes" | K1.6: "Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation"
cells.cite: K1.6, §28.9, §30.14 (string/Type bullet; function types; boxed values)
cells.note: `string` and `Type` cross as shared immutable references, a boxed value only if its type is sendable, and a function value never; none carries an obligation, so no cross-domain disposal question arises. Hunted: a function value smuggling captured owned bindings across (never sendable, and spawn entries are capture-free).

cells.rule: §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type." | K3.9: "or at the call (for `DisposeAsync()`, logical disposal completes at the returned task's terminal state and reclamation follows there" | §28.2: "`Dispose()` on any class instance is idempotent: the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops." | §28.12: "A second call to `Dispose()` or `DisposeAsync()` after either has run is a no-op ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence rule). The runtime tracks completion at the granularity of the object, not per-method." | §28.12: "the class's two cleanup paths are alternatives, not a sequence" | §28.12: "physical reclamation runs **exactly once, immediately after whichever logical-disposal path completes**" | §28.2: "The compiler additionally **must** emit a compile-time warning when a local variable is used (read, borrowed from, or consumed) after an explicit `Dispose()` or direct `DisposeAsync()` call" | §30.1: "every borrow source reaching an async call must outlive the settlement of the returned task"
cells.note: A direct `DisposeAsync()` on an owned binding is a K3.9 kill whose logical disposal completes only at the returned task's terminal state. The text does not decide what a second disposal call issued inside that window does. Reading A, §28.2 ('the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops'): a no-op. Reading B, §28.12 ('after either has run'; 'tracks completion'): the synchronous path runs the destructor and reclamation while DisposeAsync is suspended, and when it completes reclamation 'follows there' again. That runs both 'alternative' cleanups and frees twice. §28.2's warning on the repeated call does not reject it. Implicit discharge (auto-drop, unwind) is decided: synchronous, never awaits (L4-RC3).

cells.rule: §28.12: "**The `DisposeAsync` awaited is the run-time object's.**" | §28.12: "Over an owned right-hand side with no `DisposeAsync` to await — a value-type, runtime-managed or move-only right-hand side, or an object whose class does not implement `IAsyncDisposable` — scope exit takes the synchronous disposal (or the no-op) and likewise awaits nothing." | §30.7: "On **early abandonment** — the consumer disposes a suspended iterator — [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s synchronous disposal pass takes [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s synchronous-fallback path for every `await using var` active at the suspension point" | §28.6: "the scope-end machinery of a `using var` or `await using var` whose `DisposeAsync()` was called directly skips it like any explicitly-disposed binding" | §28.12: "A second call to `Dispose()` or `DisposeAsync()` after either has run is a no-op ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence rule). The runtime tracks completion at the granularity of the object, not per-method." | §28.2: "`Dispose()` on any class instance is idempotent: the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops."
cells.cite: A5, §28.6, §28.10, §28.12 (await using; run-time object; sync fallback), §29.7, §30.7; #5653, #5654 (impl)
cells.note: `await using var` is decided on every edge it owns. It awaits the run-time object's `DisposeAsync` on the normal and exception edges of an async body and disposes synchronously when there is nothing to await. Early iterator abandonment takes the synchronous fallback, with §30.7 rejecting fallback-less types across a yield, and a borrow-pin awaits nothing. Open only through the direct call: `c.DisposeAsync()` on the pinned binding is admitted, its scope end then skips it, and a second disposal call inside the in-flight window has R1/C14's two readings (L4-RC3).

cells.rule: §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §28.3: "A temporary that is instead bound (to a `var`/`using var`), `move`d, returned, or transferred into an owning location is governed by the corresponding transfer or discharge rule and is **not** disposed under this rule (it would otherwise be disposed twice)." | §28.12: "A `DisposeAsync()` task that is itself abandoned without an await (e.g. `using var t := obj.DisposeAsync();` with no await) still runs to its terminal state"
cells.cite: K8.1, §28.3 (Unbound owned temporaries), §28.12 (Implicit discharge is synchronous; abandoned DisposeAsync task), §17.13, A6
cells.note: A temporary's boundary disposal is an implicit path and always synchronous, so an `IAsyncDisposable` temporary takes the destructor path (the no-destructor warning covers the class side). `await using var _ := e;` is R2. `Make().DisposeAsync()` mints a Task temporary that may not be discarded (A6) and, when abandoned, still runs to its terminal state, with reclamation following there. The receiver-side boundary question is R3/C9's.

cells.rule: §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type." | §28.6: "The call is an **early release point**, not a discharge of the slot's obligation: the slot keeps its reference and its [K9](#sec-kernel-k9) obligation, and the containing object's teardown still runs the cascade over it ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) step 2), where the second call is [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s no-op" | §28.12: "A second call to `Dispose()` or `DisposeAsync()` after either has run is a no-op ([§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s idempotence rule). The runtime tracks completion at the granularity of the object, not per-method." | §28.2: "`Dispose()` on any class instance is idempotent: the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops." | §28.12: "**Physical reclamation** runs once, after logical disposal has completed: owned fields are disposed in reverse declaration order, the base class's reclamation chains, and the heap block is released."
cells.cite: §28.4, §28.6, §28.12 (steps 1–2; Implicit discharge is synchronous; fallback warning), §30.1
cells.note: The cascade over an `owned` field is implicit and synchronous, never awaiting, so an async-only cleanup is skipped and the class is warned at its declaration. The declaring type's direct `_f.DisposeAsync()` is an early release. Awaited, the later cascade call is the R4/C9 second call (L4-RC1). Not awaited, the owner's teardown issues a synchronous `Dispose()` while `_f.DisposeAsync` is suspended, and nothing warns because the receiver is a field. Whether that call is a no-op or runs the destructor and a second reclamation is R1/C14's open question (L4-RC3).

cells.rule: §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §28.6: "an element borrow of an **owning** collection (`pool[i].Dispose()` — use `Remove`/`RemoveAt`, the indexer-set, or `move coll[i]`, whose forms keep the slot state coherent" | §28.6: "`Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error."
cells.note: Container cascades, `Remove`/`Clear` and the indexer-set's displacement are implicit and synchronous. An element's own `DisposeAsync()` through an element borrow is the borrow-receiver error. Asynchronous per-element cleanup is spelled by taking the element out (`Drain()`, `Pop*`, `move coll[i]`) into an owned binding and using `await using` on it, which is R1/R2.

cells.rule: §28.12: "Over an owned right-hand side with no `DisposeAsync` to await — a value-type, runtime-managed or move-only right-hand side, or an object whose class does not implement `IAsyncDisposable` — scope exit takes the synchronous disposal (or the no-op) and likewise awaits nothing." | §35.9: "`Dispose` stays off the surface everywhere: choices do not implement `IDisposable`" | §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown"
cells.note: Move-only values have no `DisposeAsync`, so `await using var` over one awaits nothing and disposes slots or payloads synchronously. An `IAsyncDisposable` payload or slot object is disposed by its holder's implicit, synchronous pass.

cells.rule: §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §30.9: "The exception is disposed **exactly once, by the task that owns it, when the task is disposed**" | §31.1: "the runtime's dispose-after-arm sets the disposed flag, so a borrow surviving the handler faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode"
cells.note: Task teardown's disposal of an unconsumed result, a task's disposal of its owned fault exception, and the runtime's dispose-after-arm all run from synchronous, implicit positions and take the synchronous path. A Pattern B result is handed to the awaiter, which may `await using` it (R2). Note: the dispose-after-arm path is not in §28.12's enumerated list, but nothing at those positions can await.

cells.rule: §30.7: "On **early abandonment** — the consumer disposes a suspended iterator — [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s synchronous disposal pass takes [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s synchronous-fallback path for every `await using var` active at the suspension point" | §30.7: "therefore **may not be live across a `yield return`** in an async iterator" | §29.1: "a `Dispose()`/`DisposeAsync()` after an advance whose value was never taken **disposes the pending value**" | §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown"
cells.cite: K6, §28.12, §29.7, §29.8, §30.1, §30.7 (await for; await in finally; yield-liveness rule), §29.1; #5654 (impl), #5657
cells.note: `await for` acquires the async enumerator under `await using`. Early abandonment runs §29.7's synchronous pass with the per-binding synchronous fallback, `await` in a source-written `finally` of an async iterator is rejected, and fallback-less `await using` bindings may not be live across a yield. An untaken pending value is disposed by `DisposeAsync()` as by `Dispose()`. Frame teardown of `owned` parameters is implicit and synchronous. Hunted: disposing an async enumerator while a `MoveNextAsync` task is pending violates the §30.1 settlement clause on the receiver, and the resumption's field access faults in checked mode (L5's columns).

cells.rule: §22.13: "Static `owned` fields are disposed at program exit, after `Main` completes" | §22.13: "the destructors the pass invokes" | §22.13: "No other Bezel code runs concurrently during the shutdown sequence" | §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type." | §22.12 rule 4: "the referenced instance is reachable from every domain, and confining its use to one domain — or ensuring its own internal synchronization — is the programmer's obligation (the checked-disposal backstop of [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract) applies; this is the singleton-with-resources pattern the warning text names)."
cells.cite: §22.12 rule 4, §22.13 (Disposal of static owned fields; shutdown thread), §28.6, §28.12
cells.note: The implicit path is decided. The exit pass runs on the shutdown thread, invokes destructors (synchronous), and runs alone. The explicit path is not: the declaring type's direct `DisposeAsync()` on a `static owned` field is admitted (§28.6) and leaves a logically disposed object in always-live, every-domain storage. The exit pass then disposes it a second time, synchronously. R9/C9 and R9/C13 hold the open questions; this cell adds that the in-flight window of an unawaited call is visible to other domains too (L4-RC2, L4-RC3).

cells.rule: §28.12: "Over an owned right-hand side with no `DisposeAsync` to await — a value-type, runtime-managed or move-only right-hand side, or an object whose class does not implement `IAsyncDisposable` — scope exit takes the synchronous disposal (or the no-op) and likewise awaits nothing." | K1.6: "Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation"
cells.note: `await using var` over a runtime-managed value takes the no-op and awaits nothing, and no runtime-managed type carries an obligation for an async path to discharge.
