cells.rule: K3.5 row: "at the await, on all outgoing edges including fault and cancel" | §30.5: "the await consumes the task as part of the operation and satisfies the discharge requirement on the operand — **on all outgoing edges of the await, including the fault/cancel (exception) edge**" | §30.5: "A **named** operand — a `using var` or plain owned local, an `owned` parameter, an `owned` field — is **borrow-awaited**: the await neither consumes nor disposes it" | §30.5: "the await's implicit task disposal sets the disposed flag, so a stale borrow of the operand faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode" | §30.5: "A bare `var x := await someTask;` compiles: `x` is an owned local under the standard [§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows) discharge rules" | §30.9: "A faulted task **owns its fault exception**." | §30.9: "a task disposed while its own fault exception is in flight defers that disposal until the exception's handling completes (so a `using var`-bound task unwound by its own fault never destroys the exception mid-dispatch)"
cells.cite: K3.5, K4.2, §30.2, §30.3 (`.Result` on `OwningTask<T>`), §30.4, §30.5 (consumer-side rules; Pattern B), §30.9 (fault ownership), §28.2, §28.12
cells.note: Decided legs: a Pattern B result bound by `var x := await t` is an ordinary owned local (auto-drop/exception path); an owned `OwningTask<T>` operand is consumed by K3.5 on every edge, fault and cancel included, and the await's disposal flag backstops stale borrows (K4.2); a named `Task`/`Task<T>` operand is borrow-awaited and keeps its own discharge; a frame-held borrow of the binding is §30.1's recorded settlement clause. Open leg (RC-L5-3): an owned task local awaited and faulted, whose instance escapes the `async` body uncaught — the local's auto-drop is deferred "until the exception's handling completes", while the instance faults the enclosing task, which §30.9's first sentence makes its owner too: two owners of one instance, and no handling-completes event inside the frame.

cells.rule: §28.12: "always take the synchronous `Dispose()` path, on every edge and in every context including `async` bodies: an implicit disposal point never awaits" | §30.5: "disposed at the end of the **innermost enclosing block** on every exit edge, exactly as a hand-written `using var` at the same line would be" | §30.5: "the await's implicit disposal happens first, and the using-var's disposal at scope end is a no-op per the idempotency rule" | §30.5: "the chained-slot arrangement **defers its disposal** from the frame's scope end to the outer task's teardown" | §30.5: "On both paths the source task is disposed exactly once — by the outer task's destructor, transitively." | §30.1: "Disposing a not-yet-settled task does not cut this short: the underlying operation runs to its terminal state" | §30.9: "a task disposed while its own fault exception is in flight defers that disposal until the exception's handling completes (so a `using var`-bound task unwound by its own fault never destroys the exception mid-dispatch)"
cells.cite: §28.10, §28.12, §30.5 (scoped await-bind; Pattern A kind 2; Pattern B borrowed operand), A12, §30.1, §30.9, §30.10, #5653 (await using over a static type, C14)
cells.note: Decided legs: a `using var` live across an `await` is disposed synchronously at its block's end on every edge (§28.12); the scoped await-bind's hidden slot is a hand-written `using var` at the same line; a `using var` Pattern B task awaited by borrow is disposed by the await and its scope-end disposal is the idempotent no-op (a program that relies on §28.2's idempotence, noted). Open legs: (RC-L5-2) A12 defers a `using var` source's disposal to the outer task's teardown, but if the outer task is disposed while the frame still awaits the source, that teardown has already run before the chain forms, and no text states who disposes the late-chained source; (RC-L5-3) §30.9's own `using var`-bound example — a task unwound by its own fault — defers disposal until handling completes, which never happens in a frame whose body lets the fault escape into its task.

cells.rule: §28.3: "for such an operand the disposal is deferred to the end of the full expression rather than performed at the await, so the borrowed result outlives its uses" | §30.5: "The implicit task-disposal performed by the runtime as part of the await satisfies the discharge requirement on the temporary" | K6.5: "A frame sourced by an unbound temporary must itself be consumed to its bound within the same full expression" | §30.9: "an await that consumed its operand task ... performs the deferred task disposal as its terminal act, after handling completes" | §30.9: "A faulted task **owns its fault exception**."
cells.cite: K8.1, K6.5, §28.3 (Unbound owned temporaries; Deferred-activation callees), §30.3 (`.Result`), §30.5 (consumer-side rules; scoped await-bind), §30.9
cells.note: Decided legs: a Pattern A temporary operand is disposed at its full expression's end after the borrowed result's uses; a Pattern B or no-result temporary is consumed and disposed by the await; a temporary argument to a task-minting callee is admitted only when the task is consumed to settlement within the full expression (K6.5), else rejected; on a raise before the await the K8.1 unwind disposes it. Open leg (RC-L5-3): the canonical `await Inner()` over a faulting `Inner` — the temporary's disposal is the await's terminal act "after handling completes", but the instance it owns escapes the body uncaught into the enclosing task, which §30.9 also makes its owner; if no awaiter ever handles it, no disposal moment exists (leak), and if one does, later awaiters of a multi-awaited `Task` re-raise an instance the temporary's deferred disposal may already have freed.

cells.rule: §28.8.1: "The rule reads a field of **any** object `x` — `this`, a parameter, or a local holder the method itself disposes, whose destructor would meet the hole at that same exit — in every body, an `async` or iterator body included" | K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | K1.3: "the obligation has transferred out; the binding or slot is unreadable until reassigned, and discharge machinery skips it" | §30.1: "its `this` receiver, and an `async` lambda's captures are borrows captured into the state-machine frame" | §9.4: "a read of the vacated field through an alias of its holder, which the moved-from state of [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) does not track, reads the same state" | §28.7: "A moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal"
cells.cite: K9, K9.2, K1.3, §28.8.1 (field-restoration rule; throwable inventory incl. `await`), §28.7, §30.1 (held until settlement), §9.4 (vacated move-only field), §7 (interleaving at a suspension point), #5725
cells.note: Decided legs: an owned field's obligation is the object's (cascade or drop-on-overwrite, synchronous per §28.12); `this` is held by the frame until settlement under §30.1's K4.3 clause, so a destruction of the holder mid-suspension is that clause's violation, flag-backstopped. Open leg (RC-L5-4 ii): K9.2 lets a `move this._r` window span an `await`, which opens it to every other continuation of the domain; what an alias read (or a drop-on-overwrite through another method) of a **class-typed** vacated field observes is not stated — §9.4 states it for a move-only field's whole-value move (the disposed state, faulting), §28.7 implies only that a moved-from slot is runtime-distinguishable. Reading 1: the vacated field reads as disposed and faults in checked mode (the §9.4 posture, unstated for classes); Reading 2: it reads the moved-out object (now the frame local's) or a null under a non-nullable type, with no backstop. The synchronous twin (a callee reading the field inside the window) is L3's R4/C5 question; the suspension widens the readers from callees the body calls to any continuation.

cells.rule: §30.5: "**An indexer access on an owning collection** whose static type is `OwningArray<Task<T>>` (or analogous), where the collection itself occupies an owning location." | §30.5: "When the operand is borrowed, the await still disposes the task implicitly per the runtime semantics, but no discharge is owed for it." | §30.4: "a second await raises `InvalidOperationException`, even after a successful first await" | K9.2: "every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | §28.7: "A moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal"
cells.cite: §28.11 (`move coll[i]`), §30.4, §30.5 (admitted operand positions; Pattern B borrowed operand), K9.2, K5.6, §28.7
cells.note: Decided legs: awaiting an owning-collection slot of `Task<T>` is a Pattern A borrow sourced at the collection; awaiting a slot of `OwningTask<T>` disposes the task in place (the slot keeps a disposed task, the cascade's later Dispose is the idempotent no-op, a second await raises `InvalidOperationException`, other member access meets the K4.1 flag); the drain-await idiom consumes each element task (K3.5). Open leg (RC-L5-4 ii): a `move coll[i]` window held across an `await` exposes the vacated slot to interleaved continuations; as for R4/C10, no text states what an alias read of the vacated class-typed slot observes.

cells.rule: §30.1: "Parameters of move-only value type ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)) carrying no borrows ride the same machinery" | §30.5: "declaring `Task<T>` or `OwningTask<T>` over such a T is a **compile error at the declaration**" | §15.3: "an `async` or iterator member cannot be called on a move-only receiver" | §9.4: "a read of the vacated field through an alias of its holder, which the moved-from state of [§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression) does not track, reads the same state" | §15.3: "any slot moved-from via `move arr[i]` must be reassigned before any exit edge, because auto-dispose on a moved-from slot is not defined"
cells.cite: §15.3, §15.1.1, §9.4 (disposed state of vacated storage), §30.1, §30.5 (move-only row), §35.5, K3.12, K9.2, #4883 (owning match with `await` in an arm crashes; implementation)
cells.note: Decided legs: a move-only `async` parameter rides the frame and is disposed at the terminal state; a move-only value can be no task result (rejected at the declaration) and no `async` receiver; a move-only local across an `await` is an ordinary frame-resident owned local; a whole-value `move` of a move-only field leaves §9.4's disposed state, so an interleaved alias read faults (decided). Reading A: §29.7's abandonment ends the body "as if the body had exited at the suspension point", which is "any other transfer of control that leaves the method body", so every `yield return` inside the window is an unrestored exit and the program is rejected. Reading B: the path set is the body's CFG — normal return, `throw`, `yield break`, exception edges — and a `yield return` has a resume edge, so the restoration after it satisfies the rule; then abandonment disposes `t` (a frame-resident owned local) and leaves `_r` vacated for good, which later member reads and the holder's destructor meet — the hole K9.2 exists to prevent. The listed exits name `yield break` but not `yield return`, which supports B; §29.7's wording supports A.

The state machine takes ownership at construction time. When the iterator is disposed, the state machine disposes any `owned` parameter that has not been moved out of by the body." | §29.8 (Echo): "// No using var: source is disposed by the iterator state machine when the" | §29.11: "or an `owned` parameter of the iterator body ([§29.4](#sec-lazy-evaluation)'s frame-resident-source list), [§29.2](#sec-iterator-yield-ownership)'s borrowed-expression bullet, which [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s pass disposes when the enumerator is disposed" | §29.11: "Each `GetEnumerator()` call produces an independent enumerator." | K4.3: "no new admission may be made without recording its clause or its backstop"

cells.note: Re-verified at v0.333 @ f6e9003; the pilot's verdict holds. An `owned` parameter of an iterator whose return type is re-iterable (`IEnumerable<T>`, `IOwningEnumerable<T>`, and the async forms) is taken by 'the state machine' at the call, while each `GetEnumerator()` re-runs the body from the start, and the parameter is disposed 'when the enumerator is disposed' (§29.8's own Echo comment, §29.11). No text says whether the parameter lives in the enumerable or in each enumerator, nor bars a second enumeration (§29.11's at-most-once rule is stated for lazy queries only; K6 lists the two separately). A second enumeration re-runs the body over a parameter the first enumerator disposed, or, in §29.8's own `using var r := move reader;` shape, moves an already-moved parameter again. The read is admitted statically and no K4.3 clause records it; whether it meets K4.1's flag depends on the unstated representation of a moved-from frame slot. Recommended issue: 'spec-defect: §29.3 / §29.8 (v0.333): an `owned` parameter of a re-iterable iterator is disposed by the first enumerator, and a second `GetEnumerator()` re-runs the body over it'. Body: state the holder (enumerable vs enumerator); options (a) a re-iterable iterator with an `owned` parameter is single-enumeration (affine, §29.11's static check plus runtime `InvalidOperationException`), (b) the enumerable owns the parameter, each enumerator borrows it, and a `move` of it in such a body is rejected, (c) `owned` parameters admitted only at the single-use enumerator return types. Recommend (b): it keeps §29.3's re-iterability and makes the frame (K6.1: completion or disposal of the enumerable) the one discharge point. Further hunted here: two live enumerators over one enumerable (nested `for` over `xs`) — the inner loop's enumerator disposal disposes `r` while the outer still reads it; an enumerable never enumerated — disposed with the enumerable under either holder reading. Other R8/C11 legs are decided: frame-resident owned locals and adopt-then-yield bindings are disposed by §29.7's pass; minting yields by the next advance; the frame as a minted owned value (K6.3), the lazy query's affine right (§29.11), and drain views (stdlib §4.13). #4828/#4827/#5698 are implementation trackers of decided text.

routes.rule: §33.3: "**`Environment.Exit(code)`:** callable from any domain; it initiates the same shutdown sequence (no further continuations anywhere, static `owned` disposal on the dedicated shutdown thread, then process exit with `code`). It never returns." | §33.3: "their owned state is reclaimed by the process exit, not by disposal" | §28.10: "Disposal happens on every exit path: normal completion, `break`, `return`, or exception." | §28.3: "These rules ensure that every owned class instance is disposed **exactly once** at runtime"

Reading A: no unwind, they are reclaimed by process exit like an abandoned domain's state ('Like abandonment above' points this way), which is a waiver no rule records for the calling thread. Reading B: Exit unwinds the caller (an uncatchable propagation), running `using var` disposals and `finally` blocks before the shutdown pass. §22.13 lists `Environment.Exit()` as graceful shutdown but promises only the static pass.
routes.route: Environment.Exit from inside live scopes: the calling stack's owned locals, `using var`s and pending `finally` blocks

routes.rule: §28.7: "A moved-from or null location therefore stores without disposal — which is precisely how the field-restoration rule's `move`-then-reassign idiom ([§28.8.1](#sec-the-move-expression)) stays single-disposal" | §28.8.1: "The store itself is into a moved-from location, so it is non-throwable (below)." | §28.3: "a slot kill *by move* — `move box.f` into a transfer, a spawn argument, or one of the domain-reachable constructions of the domain clause — disposes nothing and sets no flag" | §15.1.1: "leaves the field's storage in [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s disposed state until the restoration store" | K9.4: "static state is observable across method boundaries, so no per-method window can cover it"
routes.note: Between `var t := move _f;` and the restoration, code the window admits can reach the same field through `this` or another alias: a call inside a `try` whose `finally` restores (§28.8.1), an `await` (a suspension lets other continuations of the domain run), or a constructor body under `new` (not throwable, so no `finally` needed). A re-entrant read of `_f` meets a moved-from class-typed slot with no stated runtime posture (no flag is set, unlike the move-only field's §9.4 disposed state); a re-entrant store into `_f` (drop-on-overwrite) is then overwritten by the restoration, which stores 'without disposal' by rule, so the re-entrant value leaks. The same window opens on owning-collection slots and on form-(iv) static slots, where K9.4's own ground is the point.
routes.route: re-entrant access to a moved-from field or slot inside its K9.2 restoration window (finally-restoration, await, constructor callback)

routes.note: Route: an owned field (or an owning slot, via `move coll[i]`) is moved into an owned field of an object that the moved value itself transitively owns, so the owned-field graph gains a cycle that no cascade ever reaches. K1.7's one-holder rule holds at every step and the restoration rule is met, and because slot kills are outside the freeze (K5.6) a borrow of the moved object can still receive the store. The result is a silent leak: no destructor runs, no flag is set, no diagnostic fires. The chapter records the hazard only for `Shared<T>`, and no clause records it for plain owned fields.
routes.route: ownership cycle through owned fields formed by `move h.f` (or `move coll[i]`) into a field of an object the moved value owns

Meanwhile §35.4 says its destructor disposes the choice and so runs the payload's destructor. One of the two must give, and the classification is part of the API surface (§28.9).
routes.route: trivial-dispose classification of a class holding an owning-choice field

routes.rule: §28.13: "Disposing a handle decrements the count; disposing the last live handle disposes the underlying value (running its destructor cascade normally)." | §28.13: "**`TryUpgrade(): owned Shared<T>?`** atomically produces a new strong handle if the value is still alive, and `null` otherwise" | §28.2: "`Dispose()` on any class instance is idempotent: the first call performs the disposal; subsequent calls are no-ops."
routes.note: Route: `Shared<T>` last drop inside a pass. The last handle's disposal runs the underlying value's cascade under §28.4's discipline (a throwing destructor still completes the handle's own steps). Hunted: `Weak<T>.TryUpgrade()` called from the underlying value's own destructor, or from another value's destructor in the same pass, while the last drop is in progress. 'Still alive' is not defined for a value whose disposal has begun. If the upgrade succeeds, the resurrected handle's later last drop is §28.2's no-op and its `Get()` borrow meets the K4.1 flag, so exactly-once holds but rests on idempotence. Recommend an editorial clarification that the count reaches zero before the value's disposal begins, so `TryUpgrade` answers null (folded into RC6).
routes.route: `Shared<T>` last drop: `Weak<T>.TryUpgrade` during the underlying value's disposal

routes.rule: §22.13: "the destructors the pass invokes — and any **lazy static initialization** their first touches trigger, which remains permitted under [§22.12](#sec-static-members) rule 1 unchanged — are the only Bezel code executing." | §22.13: "Static `owned` fields initialized during the pass join it" | §15.1.1: "When the pass is the holder's destruction ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) step 2), it leaves the array in [§9.4](#sec-value-receivers-are-borrows)'s **disposed state**, which checked disposal mode tests on every read through a borrowing-match binding of the array"
routes.note: Route: a destructor run by the exit pass stores a fresh owned value into a slot of a form-(iv) static owning inline array that the pass has already disposed. The drain re-enrols only fields *initialized* during the pass, not slots re-populated after their field was disposed, and §9.4's disposed state is tested on reads through a borrowing-match binding, not on slot stores. The stored object is never disposed and no backstop fires. Class-typed `static owned readonly` holders do not have this problem: a member call on a disposed collection faults under K4.1.
routes.route: exit-pass re-population of an already-disposed form-(iv) static owning inline array

routes.rule: §23.3: "Assignment through a `set(owned)` property or indexer is a marker-free owned-consuming position" | §28.11: "A user-written `set(owned)` accessor over an owned field behaves identically through the ordinary owned-field assignment in its body"
routes.note: Route: the `set(owned)` accessor. The assigned value is the setter's `owned` `value` parameter. Stored into the owned field, it drops the displaced value once (§28.7). Not stored, it is auto-dropped at the setter's end with the must-use warning, and on a throw it is discharged by the setter's exception-path discharge. A setter cannot see a caller-side moved-from fact, so its drop is null-guarded at run time (cf. RC1). No escape.

routes.rule: §23.3: "Assignment through a `set(owned)` property or indexer is a marker-free owned-consuming position — the declared slot announces the consume" | K3.1: "store into an `owned` field or owning-collection slot, including through a `set(owned)` accessor ([§23.3](#sec-block-form-properties))" | §28.3: "When an owned local — or an `owned` parameter — reaches a *normal-exit* scope end without having reached a discharge point, and is not in moved-from state, it is **disposed implicitly at that scope end**"
routes.cite: K3.1, K3.14, §23.3, §28.3, §28.8.1 (raise from the consuming call)
routes.note: Route: a user `set(owned)` accessor whose body does not store `value` (or throws before storing). The caller's binding is moved-from at the assignment; inside the accessor `value` is an owned parameter, auto-dropped at the accessor's end or unwound on a raise (§28.8.1's callee-side discharge). Exactly once, no leak.
routes.route: set(owned) accessor that does not store `value`

routes.rule: §30.5: "not a `using var` binding: a `using var` cannot be moved out of ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), so a read of it is a borrow" | §31.1: "a *borrowed* class reference is not a valid operand" | A5: "`using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable, never movable out"
routes.note: Route: the two keyword kills that move an obligation, `throw u` and a Pattern B `await t`, applied to a `using var`. Both read the pinned binding as a borrow, so `throw u` is rejected (the operand must be owned) and `await t` takes §30.5's borrowed-operand case, leaving the scope-end disposal as the single discharge. No double disposal.
routes.route: throw / Pattern B await over a `using var`

routes.rule: §29.3: "An iterator method's return type is `IEnumerable<T>` (re-iterable: each call to `GetEnumerator()` runs the body again from the start)" | §29.8: "When the iterator is disposed, the state machine disposes any `owned` parameter that has not been moved out of by the body." | §29.8 (Echo): "// No using var: source is disposed by the iterator state machine when the"
routes.note: Explicit kills on the two frames of a re-iterable iterator with an `owned` parameter. The text does not say whether the parameter is discharged by the enumerator's kill (§29.8's Echo comment) or the enumerable's ('the state machine'). A second `GetEnumerator()` between the two kills re-runs the body over the disposed or moved parameter. Same root cause as the pilot's R8/C11. File under the pilot's recommended issue, not a new one.
routes.route: explicit Dispose() of a re-iterable iterator's enumerable vs its enumerators when the iterator takes an `owned` parameter
routes.issue: pilot R8/C11 recommended issue (not yet filed)

routes.rule: §28.13: "the underlying value is still disposed exactly once, by whichever domain drops the last handle" | §30.13: "each `Shared<T>` handle's drop happens-before the destruction performed by the *last* drop" | stdlib §2.16: "`Weak<T>` and `Shared<T>` of any other `T` remain domain-local"
routes.note: `Shared<T>` handles cross domains only for synchronized-set `T`. The last drop, in whichever domain, disposes the value exactly once, with every handle's drop happening-before that destruction. `Weak<T>` is always domain-local and `TryUpgrade` is atomic. A `Get()` borrow is bounded by its handle. A field-held borrow of a handle later moved away is the recorded domain clause.
routes.route: Shared<T> last-handle drop in another domain (C12/C13 route; holder rows R1/R2/R4/R5)

routes.rule: §30.12: "in **checked disposal mode** the runtime must detect destruction of a lock with live guards (holders or waiters) and fault deterministically" | §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type."
routes.note: For a `static owned readonly Locked<T>`/`RwLocked<T>` disposed early by its declaring type while another domain holds or awaits a guard, §30.12 names a checked-mode runtime detection ('a lock reached through storage the body did not bind'), and later access through a surviving guard faults off the interior's flag. This is the one static type with a stated cross-domain backstop. It also marks what L4-RC2 lacks for the other suppression-set types, and it says nothing about an acquisition begun after the destruction.
routes.route: early explicit disposal of a static data-owning lock with guards live in another domain

routes.rule: §28.6: "at a **trivial-dispose** slot type, the compiler's single free stays at the holder's release point, which [§28.9](#sec-trivial-dispose-classes) already fixes as the containing object's teardown, the explicit call having performed logical disposal only." | §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field / owning-collection slot / `static owned` field read by code of the owning object's declaring type."
routes.note: At a trivial-dispose field type, an explicit early `Dispose()` performs logical disposal only (sets the flag). The single free stays at the holder's release point, so the teardown's later call reads a live flag in both modes. This is the carve L4-RC1 recommends generalizing.
routes.route: explicit early release of a trivial-dispose owned field

routes.rule: §28.6: "in the body of a `DisposeAsync` override itself, not in a lambda nested in it, `base.DisposeAsync()` is [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal) step 2's chain, not a disposal of `this`, and is admitted" | §28.12: "an override that does not chain forgoes that level's asynchronous cleanup, and its destructor body is skipped all the same" | §28.12: "**Physical reclamation** runs once, after logical disposal has completed: owned fields are disposed in reverse declaration order, the base class's reclamation chains, and the heap block is released."
routes.note: A `DisposeAsync` override's `base.DisposeAsync()` is a step of the logical disposal already under way and triggers no reclamation. An override that does not chain forgoes the base level's async cleanup by statement. Calling it twice re-runs user code, not a language obligation, because owned fields are disposed once by physical reclamation. No language-managed obligation is doubled or leaked.
routes.route: the chained base.DisposeAsync() in a DisposeAsync override (zero, one or two calls)

routes.rule: A15: "the disposal of a self-returned frame runs `Dispose()` without reclaiming" | §29.1: "The disposal of a self-returned frame therefore **runs the object's `Dispose()` and does not reclaim it**" | §29.1: "so the object is reclaimed exactly once however many times its enumerator face is taken and disposed — including when the receiver is a borrow the caller does not own" | K4.1: "in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) any later use through any alias faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException`"
routes.note: A `for` over a borrowed self-returning enumerator takes "ownership" of `this` through `GetEnumerator()` and its `__enumerator` disposal logically disposes the owner's object at loop end, reclaim left to the owner: the destructor runs once (idempotent Dispose), and the owner's later use — a second `for`, a member call — faults under K4.1 with no static warning. Recorded by axiom A15, so not opened; worth noting that the program relies on §28.2's idempotence and that the owner learns of the logical disposal only at run time (the same holds for a `static owned readonly` self-returning enumerator, single domain).
routes.route: A15 self-returning enumerator: a loop's enumerator disposal logically disposes a borrowed receiver its owner still holds

routes.rule: §30.11: "**Task-object ownership.** The **source owns the task object** its `Task` property exposes." | §30.11: "For either kind, a **never-awaited** task is disposed exactly once, by the source at source disposal." | §30.11: "A source disposed before completion first faults the task (below) and then disposes it" | §30.11: "If `TrySetResult` returns `false` because the task is already in a terminal state, the implementation disposes `result` before returning."
routes.cite: §30.11 (Task-object ownership; Common semantics; four-condition carve), A10, §30.5, §30.9
routes.note: The completion source owns its task; awaits borrow it (Pattern B awaits dispose it in place, the source's later disposal is the idempotent no-op); a never-awaited task is disposed once with the source; a source disposed before completion faults then disposes the task, deferring the fault instance's disposal past queued awaiters; a losing `TrySet*` disposes its owned argument. The callback capture is A10's named carve under four compiler-checkable conditions, with a one-shot obligation whose violation the checked-mode flag catches. No escape found.
routes.route: §30.11 completion-source carve: task object owned by the source; late completion and source disposal
